source.title_on_document: Searching together: Human–AI complementarities in innovation search

supplement.holds: No supplement or online appendix is referenced anywhere in the 16 pages. Appendix 1 (companies and positions of the interviewees, p. 14) and Appendix 2 (secondary data sources, p. 15) are in this PDF.

paper_design_summary: An exploratory qualitative study: the authors held 41 semi-structured interviews (1422 minutes in total) with employees of an AI innovation-search firm ('Firm AI'), staff of 25 of its client organizations, and staff of one non-client organization, and they analyzed 64 secondary articles on AI search tools. They coded this material with grounded-theory (Gioia) methods into three human-AI 'relational dialectics'. Nobody was assigned to AI, and no output was produced under study conditions or scored for creativity or diversity.

studies.label: Qualitative interview study plus secondary articles (AI use in innovation search)

assignment.what_was_assigned: Nothing was assigned and there are no arms. Firm AI was chosen by purposeful sampling, the 25 client organizations were identified through Firm AI's customer network (network sampling), and one non-client organization was added for triangulation.
assignment.quote: We used an exploratory qualitative research design to identify emerging complementarities between humans and AI in innovation search.
assignment.locator: p. 4, Section 3 (Method); sampling in p. 4, Section 3.1

participants.exclusions: No participant exclusions are reported; there was no experimental assignment. The paper reports 41 interviews (p. 5, Section 3.1) and 27 companies (p. 2, Section 1), but no explicit total of distinct people. Counting the entries in Appendix 1 yields 40 listed interviewees: 39 position-code rows (F1-F5 and M1-M34), with M17A/B explicitly covering two interviewees (an R&D Director and an R&D team member). F1 and M6 were each interviewed in two rounds (p. 14, Appendix 1). The appendix-derived people count is not entered as n_analyzed because the paper prints no people total.
participants.who: Innovation and R&D professionals: business development, technology and innovation scouting, innovation, and R&D managers, a chief information officer, and a chief scientist, plus four non-managerial members of innovation or R&D teams. Five are Firm AI employees (coded F), including its CEO and its co-founder. The others (coded M) work at 25 client organizations and one non-client organization.
participants.country: Europe (mainly Netherlands, Germany, Finland, Sweden, Switzerland, Belgium, Italy, UK), USA, and Saudi Arabia (Appendix 1)
participants.quote: In total, we conducted 41 interviews, amounting to 1422 min (see Appendix 1), with an average duration of 35 min per interview.

ai_tool.name_model: Alpha AI, Firm AI's NLP-based search system that scans scientific publications, patents, and company websites. Interviewees were also invited to reflect on generative AI tools such as ChatGPT, and the secondary articles cover tools such as Azure OpenAI Service, Amazon Kendra, and Glean chat.
ai_tool.how_used: Used in the interviewees' ordinary innovation-search work (technology scouting, patent and literature search) and described in interviews. The researchers did not manipulate it.

task.description: Innovation search in firms (finding technologies, patents, partners, and solutions), as described by the interviewees. The researchers set no task.
task.duration: Interviews averaged 35 minutes (1422 minutes over 41 interviews).

company_involvement.description: Firm AI, the European AI search vendor that built Alpha AI (the focal tool), was the research site. The authors used its customer network to identify the 25 client organizations, and five Firm AI employees were interviewed, including its CEO and its co-founder and managing director. The firm is not named. The document states no company author, funder, or company role in design, analysis, or writing, and it has no funding statement. The authors declare no competing interests.
company_involvement.locator: p. 4, Section 3.1; p. 14, Appendix 1 and Declaration of competing interest

eligibility.reason: Criterion 1 is not met: this exploratory qualitative interview study used purposeful and network sampling, with no assignment to AI and no experimental comparison group (p. 4, Sections 3-3.1; p. 5, Section 3.1). Criterion 2 is not met: the authors report 41 interviews but no explicit total of distinct people analyzed (p. 5, Section 3.1). Counting Appendix 1 gives 40 listed interviewees, below 50: there are 39 position-code rows (F1-F5 and M1-M34), and M17A/B covers two people (p. 14, Appendix 1). This is an appendix-derived count, so participants.n_analyzed remains null. Criterion 3 is not met: the interviews and 64 secondary articles were analyzed into qualitative themes, with no creativity or diversity score on outputs produced by participants (p. 5, Sections 3.1-3.2; p. 6, Fig. 1; p. 11, Table 2; p. 15, Appendix 2). The paper fits no eligible context class: it compares no AI output with human output, compares no real outputs on creativity or diversity, and is not a review. It remains out of scope as a qualitative study of practitioners' experiences.

one_line_finding: From 41 interviews with innovation professionals at 27 organizations (p. 2; p. 5, Section 3.1), the authors identify three human-AI relational dialectics in innovation search (human-centered vs boundary-spanning search, contextualizing vs de-contextualizing, judging vs envisaging; Fig. 1, p. 6; Table 2, p. 11), and the paper reports no quantitative creativity or diversity outcome.
notes: Data availability: 'The authors do not have permission to share data.' (p. 15). The paper mentions homogenization only in its limitations, citing Doshi and Hauser (2024) (p. 13). The AI studied is mainly Alpha AI, an NLP search system. Generative AI enters through the interviewees' reflections and the secondary articles (p. 5, Section 3.1). The search record guessed with_ai, but the paper has no quantitative outcome. Organization count: the introduction says 27 companies (p. 2), Section 3.1 describes Firm AI, 25 client organizations, and one non-client organization (pp. 4-5), and Appendix 1 lists Firm AI and 26 lettered companies (A to Z1, with no W). assignment.structure is coded 'between' only because the form offers no not-applicable value. The study has no arms.

The authors declare no competing interests.' Locator: p. 4, Section 3.1; p. 14, Appendix 1 and Declaration of competing interest.
differences.b: false. The authors declare no competing interests.' Locator: p. 4, Section 3.1; p. 14, Declaration of competing interest.
differences.resolved: true, as in A. The forms agree on the facts and differ only on the code. The AI vendor whose system (Alpha AI) is the focal tool was the research site, its customer network was the sampling frame for the 25 client organizations, and its CEO (F1, interviewed in two rounds) and its co-founder and managing director (F4) are among the five Firm AI interviewees. That is a company role in the research even without funding or authorship, and an earlier reconciled form codes a research partnership with an AI company as involvement (c003). The description keeps B's points: the firm is unnamed, no company author or funder is stated, and the authors declare no competing interests. A's word 'recruited' is replaced by the paper's 'identify'.
